claims.text: A hybrid CALPHAD–machine-learning framework can predict melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad high-entropy-alloy composition space.
The intended material domain is single, disordered solid-solution HEAs containing 4–8 metallic elements at 10–35 at % each and exhibiting no long-range ordering.
Assessed binary and ternary liquid-solution models provide the lower-order CALPHAD basis for the framework.
A machine-learning regression model trained on experimental fusion and liquid-phase data can be used to adjust multicomponent interaction parameters.
The proposed applicability conditions are ambient pressure, inert atmosphere, equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions, and temperatures bracketing the predicted melting point.
Liquid-phase behavior is mediated by configurational entropy and excess-Gibbs-energy terms supplemented by ML-derived higher-order interaction corrections.
Nonlinear multicomponent effects are absent or inadequately represented in lower-order CALPHAD assessments.
Machine-learned interaction corrections compensate for these missing nonlinear multicomponent effects.
Correcting the liquid free-energy surfaces improves calculated phase equilibria and fusion properties.
At least 80% of tested HEAs will have predicted melting temperatures within ±50 K of experiment.
At least 80% of tested HEAs will have predicted enthalpies and entropies of fusion within ±10% of experiment.
At least 80% of tested HEAs will have predicted volume changes at melting within ±5% of experiment.
Standard CALPHAD based only on binary and ternary data typically has approximately ±100 K melting-temperature error.
Standard CALPHAD based only on binary and ternary data typically has 20–30% error in fusion enthalpy.
The approach may fail for alloys containing ordered intermetallic phases or strong short-range order absent from the training set.
Prediction uncertainty increases outside the 4–8-element and 10–35 at % per-element domain.
Model variance indicates melting-temperature uncertainty of ±20–40 K and fusion-enthalpy uncertainty of ±5–15%.
Differential scanning calorimetry can measure melting temperature and integrated enthalpy of fusion for the proposed validation.
Entropy of fusion can be obtained as ΔH/Tm.
High-temperature dilatometry can determine volume change at melting for the proposed validation.

contradictions.description: The performance claim requires at least 80% of alloys to meet ±50 K, ±10%, and ±5% thresholds, but falsification requires more than 50% to exceed much looser ±100 K, ±20%, or ±10% thresholds. The claimed performance could therefore fail decisively without triggering the stated falsification rule.

The hypothesis covers entropy of fusion and general liquid-phase thermodynamic properties, but the falsification rule supplies no threshold for entropy of fusion or liquid-phase density and does not test other liquid thermodynamic properties.
